background.definition: Granuloma annulare (GA) is a benign, asymptomatic, annular lesion found most commonly over the dorsum of hands, ankles, elbows, or knees. Lesions may be localized or disseminated and can occur anywhere on the body. Lesions often appear orange-red in color with central clearing to make its ringlike configuration.

Oval-shaped or elliptical-shaped plaques with red yellow color
Umbilicated lesions that are waxy, small papules

list.listitem: GA is a benign condition. The clinical diagnosis is based on appearance of raised annular lesions without scale found over the dorsum of the hands, ankles, knees, and elbows. There are 4 subtypes with different qualities and distributions (see ).
History should include questions related to onset, duration, location, and character of lesion or lesions. Ask about diabetes, insulin resistance, cancer, infection, and rheumatoid arthritis.
Look for scale that is seen with tinea corporis but not with GA.

In one retrospective review of 42 children with GA, lesions were in a single location in 23 patients (54.7%), in 2 locations in 7 patients (16.6%), and in 3 or more locations in 12 patients (28.5%). Dorsa of the hands (18 cases) and feet (11 cases) were the most common locations, followed by legs (5), ankles (3), and wrists (2).

In one case series, 34 patients (21 girls, 13 boys; average age at diagnosis = 4.6 years) were found to have subcutaneous GA. Most lesions occurred in the lower extremities, especially in a pretibial location.
Skin biopsy is not needed in most cases because the clinical picture is clear. When the diagnosis is not certain, a 4-mm punch biopsy will provide adequate tissue for a definitive diagnosis.
When tinea corporis is a consideration, perform a KOH preparation to look for hyphae.
A punch biopsy for histology can make the definitive diagnosis.
Localized GA can be treated with injections of 5 to 10 mg/mL intralesional triamcinolone acetonide into the elevated borders only; repeated injections may be required. C
A case series reported successful use of cryotherapy for localized GA. C

Disseminated GA may be treated with oral dapsone 100 mg daily, zileuton 2400 mg daily plus vitamin D 400 IU daily, oral isotretinoin, or oral pentoxifylline, although data are limited to small case series and case reports. C
Topical steroids alone or with occlusion have been used to treat GA. Evidence of their effectiveness is lacking.

Inject 5 to 10 mg/mL intralesional triamcinolone acetonide into the elevated borders only. Repeated injections may be required. Although there are a few case reports, evidence of effectiveness is lacking.

The use of dapsone by mouth 100 mg daily for disseminated GA is based on case reports. Avoid dapsone in G6PD deficiency. In one case report the patient reported a clear improvement of the pruritus after 2 weeks and improvement of the skin was observed after 2 months. Clinical symptoms improved gradually and the only residual lesions remaining after 12 months of treatment with dapsone were macules and brown marks; no lesions remained after 15 months.
Oral isotretinoin has been used to treat disseminated GA, but only case reports have been reported so far. Some patients have relapsed after treatment.
Three patients with disseminated GA were treated successfully with zileuton 2400 mg plus vitamin E 400 IU by mouth daily.
In a case report, one patient with generalized GA was successfully treated with oral pentoxifylline daily.
A systematic review summarized therapeutic options but confirmed a lack of evidence-based treatment for generalized GA.

Cryosurgery was studied prospectively in 31 patients with localized GA. The patients were treated by cryosurgery, using the contact method with nitrous oxide or liquid nitrogen. Each lesion was treated with one freeze-thaw cycle of 10 to 60 seconds per session applied with closed probes. If needed, treatment was repeated after 20 to 30 days.

Resolution of the lesions was obtained in all patients, and resolution after a single freeze-thaw cycle occurred in 25 of 31 patients (80.6%). Relapse occurred in only 1 of the 11 patients who were followed up for more than 2 years; the relapse occurred 16 months after treatment.

UVA1 340 to 400 nm phototherapy provided good or excellent results in 10 of 20 patients with disseminated GA. However, discontinuation of treatment was followed by early recurrence of GA in the majority of patients.
PUVA showed clearance or good improvement of generalized GA in 66% of cases. Prolonged remission occurred in less than a third of patients.
Pulsed dye laser (585 nm) was successfully used in one patient but required 3 treatments over 13 months to achieve remission.
GA may be self-limiting but can be persistent and recurrent. Disseminated GA can be troublesome for years. C
In children, spontaneous remission occurs in 90% of cases over a median of 12 months, but re thecurrence rate is high (38%) irrespective of treatment. B

tr.td: This is the most common form of granuloma annulare. Typically presents on the dorsal surfaces of extremities, especially of the back of the hands, the ankles, feet, knees, and elbows.
Adults are most affected by this form which begins in the extremities and can spread to the trunk and neck.

Children and young adults present with one to hundreds of 1- to 4-mm annular papules that may coalesce to form a typical annular plaque. This form has an affinity for extremities, especially the hands and fingers.

These lesions present as rapidly growing, nonpainful, subcutaneous or dermal nodules on the extremities, scalp, and forehead. Subcutaneous GA mainly affects children. The lesions are deeper so more swelling is seen with less annular definition.
